intro: Lawyer burnout from billable hour pressure is common, and survey data backs that up. In a 2025 ALM and Law.com Compass survey of more than 3,100 lawyers and staff, 65.5% said billable-hour pressure hurts their mental well-being. This page covers the costs, the causes and the fixes you can start on your Mac today, without buying anything.
tldr: 65.5% of lawyers and staff in a 2025 survey said billable-hour pressure hurts their mental well-being.
Burnout often shows up alongside anxiety, depression and heavy drinking. The 2016 ABA and Hazelden Betty Ford study found high rates of each.
The money costs are hard to measure from the sources used here, so this page does not invent numbers for them.
A model that bills by the hour rewards logged time, and email keeps the clock running after hours.
Start with a one week hour log, a stop time and one email rule. Then take the log to a supervising lawyer.

blocks.text: What billable hour pressure does to lawyers

Billable hour pressure is the push to log more chargeable time every week. It reaches into evenings, weekends and sleep. Over time it can turn into burnout. Burnout is long-running exhaustion, growing cynicism about the work, and a sense that nothing you do is enough.

Burnout is a pattern tied to work. It is not a diagnosis. Depression and anxiety are medical conditions, and they can overlap with burnout. The survey on this page measured well-being, depression and anxiety, so keep those ideas separate when you check yourself.

The most recent figure comes from the ALM and Law.com Compass survey, published May 15, 2025. It drew on more than 3,100 lawyers and staff, mostly at BigLaw firms. Respondents said billable-hour pressure hurts their mental well-being at a rate nearly four points higher than in 2024. That is a rise, not a fall.

Keep the sample in mind. A survey of mostly large-firm lawyers does not describe every practice. A solo practitioner, a public defender and an in-house lawyer may feel the pressure differently. The sources here do not settle that comparison for every role.
Lawyer burnout signs to check for this week

Check yourself the way you would check a client file. Look for patterns that last several weeks, not one heavy week. The signs below are common descriptions of burnout. They are not a test, and only a doctor can assess your health.

items: You dread opening your inbox before you have had your first coffee.
You log time late at night to catch up on the day's entries.
Cases or clients that used to matter now feel numb or distant.
You drink more than you planned in order to wind down.
You feel guilty when you take a full day off.
You sleep badly, or you get sick more often than you used to.

blocks.text: If several of these match, book a visit with a doctor. Tell them about your work hours, sleep and drinking, not only your mood. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, contact emergency services or a crisis line in your country now.
The costs of billable hour pressure, and the gaps in the data

The costs fall into three groups: mental health, drinking and missed help. Money, write-offs and career damage matter too. The sources used here did not give reliable figures for those, so this page does not guess at them.

blocks.text: Read the drinking figures with care. The 2016 ABA and Hazelden Betty Ford study measured lawyers across the profession. The chart below breaks problem drinking into groups. A group rate shows where the strain sits. It does not prove that billing causes the drinking.

Younger lawyers, junior associates and private-firm lawyers show higher rates in the study. That pattern fits the idea that little control over hours adds strain. It is still a pattern. The data does not test billing rules directly.

Only 6.8% of lawyers in that study sought treatment for drug or alcohol problems. Those numbers suggest many lawyers carry the strain alone. You do not need a crisis to ask for help. Asking early keeps more options open.

Ask your firm's finance team for write-off and realization reports if you want to test the money side. Those reports show what gets billed, what gets cut and where time goes unpaid. Bring the numbers to your own conversation, not to a debate about the whole profession.
Why billable hour pressure builds up in a firm

The billing model is the first cause. You get paid for time you log, so the clock sits in your head all day. Short calls, quick drafts and small emails all become entries. The day turns into a stack of small debts to clear before you can stop.

Email and phones are the second cause. In the 2025 survey, 56.3% said always being on call hurts their well-being. That figure was down 8 points. It is still more than half. A phone on the nightstand keeps the day from ever closing.

blocks.text: Firm size and practice type matter too. In a 2018 study by Koltai, Schieman and Dinovitzer, lawyers in nearly all private-sector settings reported more depressive symptoms than public-sector lawyers. Large-firm lawyers were most likely to report poor health. Higher income narrowed the gap.

Newer lawyers often carry the heaviest load. In the 2016 study, 31.1% of junior associates reported problem drinking. Junior lawyers often have the least say over their hours. That reading is mine, not a finding from the study, so test it against your own firm.
Fixes for billable hour pressure you can start without buying anything

None of these fixes needs a new app. They need a clear log, a stop time and one honest conversation. Start small. Pick one fix this week and add the next one later. Trying five changes at once usually means none of them stick.
Step 1: log every hour for one week

Use a notebook or the Notes app. Open Notes from Spotlight with ⌘ Space. For one week, write down each block of work. Note the matter, the start time, the end time and whether you could bill it. Do not fix anything yet. You are collecting facts first.

At the end of the week, sort the entries into billable, unbilled and non-billable time. Add up what each group took. Then look at the split. The unbilled part is often the hidden load, so look there first.
Step 2: set a stop time with Focus

On your Mac, open System Settings > Focus. Create a new Focus and name it Stop time. Allow only the calls you must take. Then add a schedule so it turns on at the hour you choose. Lazur can point to the Focus settings if you ask where they are.
Step 3: cut email noise with rules

In Apple Mail, open Mail > Settings > Rules and add one rule. Send newsletters and automated alerts to a folder you check once a day. In Outlook for Mac, open Outlook > Settings > Mail > Rules and do the same. Start with one sender. Rules do not stop mail from arriving. They keep it out of your way.
Step 4: bring your log to a supervising lawyer

Take the week of notes to a supervising lawyer or the managing partner. Keep the talk about workload, not blame. Ask what the expected hours are and what gets priority when two matters clash. Ask for the answer in writing if you can.

blocks.title: A talk opener that works
blocks.text: Try this: 'I logged my time for a week. I want to talk about staffing on the current matter and what my billable expectation is.' Then stop and let them answer.
Mac time tracking tools and their honest limits

A time tracker helps when logging by hand wears you down. Timing is a Mac app that tracks time automatically across apps, websites and documents. It shows unbilled time and syncs entries to Clio, so you do not enter them twice. Each entry can be set to Not Billable, Billable, Billed or Paid.

Timing offers a 30-day free trial with no credit card. Its vendor page does not list prices or the macOS version you need. Check their site for pricing before you decide. Your firm may already run a time system, so ask before you install anything.

blocks.title: Client data comes first
blocks.text: Follow your employer's rules on client and matter data before you use any tool. Lazur sends audio and screenshots to AI providers to answer. Check your firm's policy before you ask it about a client file.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥ ⌘ (Option and Command) to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It can point at things, guide you one click at a time, dictate text when you hold fn, and set reminders or calendar events by voice.

Lazur does not track your hours in the background. It does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. It is not a plugin or add-in for any app. It does not replace a time tracker or your firm's support program.

Here is where it fits. Ask where the Focus setting lives, and Lazur circles it. Ask for a draft note to your supervisor, and Lazur writes one. Hold fn to dictate your end-of-day notes into the app you already use.
Mistakes that make billable hour pressure worse

items: Logging only the billable hours. The unbilled time is where much of the load hides.
Keeping work email open all evening to look responsive.
Trying to fix everything in one week. Pick one change first.
Waiting for someone to notice. Bring facts with the feeling. A week of notes makes the talk easier to start.
Skipping the doctor because the symptoms feel normal. Lasting symptoms deserve a check-up.
Using a time tracker on client matters before checking your firm's rules.

blocks.text: Edge cases matter. A solo lawyer has no supervisor to talk to, so the fix shifts toward a stop time, a fee policy and a support contact outside the firm. A partner who sets targets can change them. A junior lawyer who raises workload should expect the talk to take more than one meeting.
What to do next

Start with the week of notes. Set a stop time and one email rule. Take the log to your supervisor before your next review. Then check the result after another week. Keep what helps and drop what does not.

If the strain lasts for weeks, or it reaches your sleep, health or drinking, see a doctor. Ask HR or your firm's wellness contact whether a confidential support program exists. Asking early keeps more options open.

faq.question: Is lawyer burnout the same as depression?
faq.answer: No. Burnout is a pattern tied to work. Depression is a medical condition, and the two can overlap. If your mood, sleep or appetite changes for weeks, see a doctor. Do not diagnose yourself from a checklist alone.

faq.question: What is a normal billable hour target for lawyers?
faq.answer: This page does not give one. The sources used here did not state a reliable target. Ask your firm for its written expectation, and ask what counts as billable work.

faq.question: Can I raise billable hour pressure with my firm without risking my job?
faq.answer: Some risk is always there, so plan the conversation carefully. Bring your hour log, keep the focus on workload, and ask for the answer in writing. Your employer's HR policy sets the rules, so check them first.

faq.question: Does Lazur track my billable hours?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is not a time tracker, and it does not run in the background. Lazur answers questions, points at things, guides you one click at a time, and drafts text. For automatic tracking, look at a dedicated time tracker like Timing.

faq.question: Is it safe to use AI tools with client files?
faq.answer: Follow your employer's rules first. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

faq.question: Where can I get confidential help with work strain?
faq.answer: Start with HR or your firm's wellness contact, and ask about a confidential support program. Your doctor is another option. In the 2016 study, only 6.8% of lawyers sought treatment for drug or alcohol problems, so asking early matters.

costs.title: Mental health strain
costs.text: 65.5% of lawyers and staff said billable-hour pressure hurts their mental well-being in the 2025 survey. 33% reported depression and 68.7% reported anxiety. These are self-reported rates from a survey, not diagnoses. They still show how widespread the strain is in that group.

costs.title: Problem drinking
costs.text: In the 2016 ABA and Hazelden Betty Ford study of 12,825 practicing lawyers, problem drinking was 20.6% for men and 15.5% for women. For lawyers aged 30 and under it was 31.9%. Those figures come from a summary of the study, not the full paper.

costs.title: Help that never happens
costs.text: Only 6.8% of lawyers in the 2016 study sought treatment for drug or alcohol problems. The gap between strain and help is the costly part. A problem handled early is usually easier to manage than one handled late.

costs.title: Money, write-offs and mistakes
costs.text: Lost income, write-offs and errors are often cited as costs of long hours. The sources used here do not give reliable figures for them. Ask your firm's finance team for write-off and realization reports, and build your case from your firm's own data.

causes.title: The hourly model rewards logged time
causes.text: You are paid for the hours you record, so the clock runs in your head all day. Short calls, quick drafts and small emails all turn into entries. That makes the day feel like a stack of small debts. The pressure is built into the model, not only into your effort.

causes.title: Email and phones keep work open
causes.text: Work reaches you after hours through the inbox and the phone. The 2025 survey found 56.3% said always being on call hurts their well-being. A message at night can feel like a deadline you already missed. Those signals rarely switch off, so the day never fully closes.

causes.title: Firm size and practice type
causes.text: Koltai, Schieman and Dinovitzer (2018) found lawyers in nearly all private-sector settings reported more depressive symptoms than public-sector lawyers. Large-firm lawyers were most likely to report poor health. Higher income narrowed the gap, which suggests money and setting are linked.

causes.title: Little say over workload when junior
causes.text: Junior associates reported problem drinking at 31.1% in the 2016 study. Junior lawyers often have the least say over staffing and deadlines. This is a reasoned reading of the pattern. The study does not test that link directly, so treat it as a hypothesis to check at your firm.

causes.title: Unclear targets and no shared limit
causes.text: When a firm sets no written hours expectation, each lawyer has to guess. Guessing tends to push people to log more and rest less. Ask for the expectation in writing, because a clear number is easier to plan around than a vague push. This is reasoning from how the pressure works, not a sourced finding.

fixes.title: Keep a one week hour log
fixes.text: Write each block of work for one week. Note the matter, the start and end times, and whether the time was billable. Sort the week into billable, unbilled and non-billable time. The unbilled share is often the hidden load. A log gives you facts for every later step.

fixes.title: Set a stop time with Focus
fixes.text: Go to System Settings > Focus on your Mac. Create a Focus named Stop time, allow only the calls you must take, and add a schedule. It is built into macOS and costs nothing. Turn it on at the end of your working day and leave it on.

fixes.title: Cut email noise with rules
fixes.text: In Apple Mail, go to Mail > Settings > Rules. In Outlook for Mac, go to Outlook > Settings > Mail > Rules. Route newsletters and automated alerts into a folder, then check that folder once a day. Start with one sender, and add more only after the first rule works.

fixes.title: Bring the log to your supervisor
fixes.text: Pick a calm time, not a deadline day. Open with the log, then ask about expected hours and priorities when matters clash. Ask for the answer in writing and keep notes of what you agreed. This turns a feeling into a plan you can both check.

fixes.title: Use support resources, not willpower alone
fixes.text: Ask HR or your firm's wellness contact whether a confidential support program exists. If your firm has none, see a doctor and describe the work pattern in plain terms. Asking early gives you more choices. Follow your employer's rules on any support you use.

fixes.title: Use a time tracker only if your firm allows it
fixes.text: Timing is a Mac time tracker with a 30-day free trial and no credit card needed. It tracks time automatically and syncs entries to Clio. Check your firm's policy first, then check the Timing site for current prices before you buy anything.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Start the hour log
plan.text: Open Notes from Spotlight with ⌘ Space. Write each block of work with the matter, start time, end time and billable status. Keep going for the whole week. Do not change anything yet.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Set your stop time
plan.text: Open System Settings > Focus. Create a Focus named Stop time, allow only the calls you must take, and add a schedule. Test it once before you rely on it.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Add one email rule
plan.text: In Apple Mail, go to Mail > Settings > Rules. Route one sender into a folder you check once a day. In Outlook for Mac, use Outlook > Settings > Mail > Rules if that is your app.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Draft your talk
plan.text: Sort the log into billable, unbilled and non-billable time. Write three lines: what you saw, what you need, and what you will try. Hold fn to dictate those lines if typing slows you down.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Have the conversation
plan.text: Meet your supervising lawyer at a calm time. Walk through the log, ask for expected hours in writing, and agree on the next check-in. Write down what you agreed before you leave the room.
